stem: Which of the following is not correct?

options.label: B
options.text: Schleiden and Schwann formulated the cell theory.

options.label: C
options.text: Virchow explained that cells are formed from pre-existing cells.

options.label: D
options.text: A unicellular organism carries out its life activities within a single cell.

solution:
**(a) Robert Brown discovered the cell.**

This statement is not correct. Robert Brown discovered the **nucleus** (1831). Anton Von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell, and the cell itself was first observed (in a thin slice of cork) and named by **Robert Hooke** (1665).

The other three statements are correct:

1. Schleiden and Schwann together formulated the cell theory.
2. Rudolf Virchow (1855) explained that new cells are formed from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula).
3. A unicellular organism is capable of independent existence and performs all the essential functions of life within its single cell.
groundedIn: §8.1; §8.2; §8.5.10 — Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell, Robert Brown discovered the nucleus (1831); Schleiden and Schwann formulated the cell theory; Virchow: new cells from pre-existing cells; unicellular organisms perform the essential functions of life; BEYOND CHAPTER: Robert Hooke first observed (in cork) and named the cell, 1665

solution:
**(c) pre-existing cells.**

Rudolf Virchow (1855) first explained that cells divide and new cells are formed from **pre-existing cells** (Omnis cellula-e cellula). This is the second tenet of the cell theory as understood today: all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Cells are not formed from abiotic materials, by fermentation or by regeneration of old cells.
groundedIn: §8.2 — Rudolf Virchow (1855) explained that cells divided and new cells are formed from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula); cell theory (ii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells

stem:
Match the following

| Column I | Column II |
|---|---|
| (a) Cristae | (i) Flat membranous sacs in stroma |
| (b) Cisternae | (ii) Infoldings in mitochondria |
| (c) Thylakoids | (iii) Disc-shaped sacs in Golgi apparatus |
solution:
(a) - (ii), (b) - (iii), (c) - (i)

| Column I | Column II |
|---|---|
| (a) Cristae | (ii) Infoldings in mitochondria |
| (b) Cisternae | (iii) Disc-shaped sacs in Golgi apparatus |
| (c) Thylakoids | (i) Flat membranous sacs in stroma |

- **Cristae** are the infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane towards the matrix; they increase the surface area.
- **Cisternae** are the flat, disc-shaped sacs of the Golgi apparatus, stacked parallel to each other.
- **Thylakoids** are the organised flattened membranous sacs present in the stroma of the chloroplast.
groundedIn: §8.5.4; §8.5.3.2; §8.5.5; Fig. 8.6; Fig. 8.7; Fig. 8.8 — inner membrane forms infoldings called cristae towards the matrix; Golgi has flat disc-shaped sacs or cisternae; thylakoids are flattened membranous sacs in the stroma

stem: Which of the following is correct:

options.label: A
options.text: Cells of all living organisms have a nucleus.

options.label: B
options.text: Both animal and plant cells have a well defined cell wall.

options.label: C
options.text: In prokaryotes, there are no membrane bound organelles.

options.label: D
options.text: Cells are formed de novo from abiotic materials.

solution:
**(c) In prokaryotes, there are no membrane bound organelles.**

Prokaryotic cells lack membrane bound organelles; the only organelles they have are ribosomes, which are not membrane bound.

The other statements are incorrect:

1. **(a)** Prokaryotic cells have no well-defined nucleus, and some mature eukaryotic cells (erythrocytes of many mammals, sieve tube cells of vascular plants) lack a nucleus.
2. **(b)** A cell wall is present in plant cells (and fungi) but absent in animal cells.
3. **(d)** All cells arise from pre-existing cells.
groundedIn: §8.3; §8.4; §8.5; §8.5.2; §8.5.10; §8.2 — prokaryotic cells lack membrane bound organelles except ribosomes; no well-defined nucleus in prokaryotes; erythrocytes of many mammals and sieve tube cells lack nucleus; cell walls absent in animal cells; all cells arise from pre-existing cells

stem: What is a mesosome in a prokaryotic cell? Mention the functions that it performs.
solution:
A **mesosome** is a special membranous structure formed by the **extensions (infoldings) of the plasma membrane into the cell**. It is a specialised, differentiated form of the cell membrane characteristic of prokaryotes, and its extensions are in the form of **vesicles, tubules and lamellae**.

**Functions of mesosomes:**

1. Help in **cell wall formation**.
2. Help in **DNA replication** and distribution of DNA to daughter cells.
3. Help in **respiration**.
4. Help in **secretion** processes.
5. Increase the **surface area** of the plasma membrane and its enzymatic content.
groundedIn: §8.4; §8.4.1 — mesosome, a specialised differentiated form of cell membrane, infoldings of cell membrane; vesicles, tubules and lamellae; help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution, respiration, secretion, increase surface area and enzymatic content

stem: How do neutral solutes move across the plasma membrane? Can the polar molecules also move across it in the same way? If not, then how are these transported across the membrane?
solution:
**Neutral solutes** move across the plasma membrane by **simple diffusion** along the concentration gradient, i.e., from higher concentration to lower concentration. This is **passive transport**, which needs no energy.

**No**, polar molecules cannot move across in the same way, because they **cannot pass through the nonpolar lipid bilayer**.

Polar molecules are transported as follows:

1. They require a **carrier protein** of the membrane to facilitate their transport across the membrane.
2. A few ions or molecules are transported **against their concentration gradient** (from lower to higher concentration). This is **active transport**, an energy dependent process in which **ATP** is utilised, e.g., the \(\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+\) pump.
groundedIn: §8.5.1 — neutral solutes move by simple diffusion along the concentration gradient (passive transport); polar molecules cannot pass through the nonpolar lipid bilayer and require a carrier protein; active transport uses ATP, e.g., Na+/K+ pump

stem: Name two cell-organelles that are double membrane bound. What are the characteristics of these two organelles? State their functions and draw labelled diagrams of both.
solution:
The two double membrane bound organelles are **mitochondria** and **chloroplasts**.

**Mitochondria: characteristics**

1. Not easily visible under the microscope unless specifically stained; their number per cell varies with the physiological activity of the cell.
2. Typically **sausage-shaped or cylindrical**, 0.2-1.0 µm in diameter (average 0.5 µm) and 1.0-4.1 µm long.
3. Bounded by an **outer membrane**, which forms the continuous limiting boundary, and an **inner membrane**, which forms infoldings called **cristae** towards the matrix; the cristae increase the surface area.
4. The two membranes divide the lumen into an outer compartment and an inner compartment; the inner compartment is filled with a dense homogeneous **matrix**.
5. The matrix has a single circular **DNA** molecule, a few RNA molecules, **70S ribosomes** and the components for protein synthesis.
6. Mitochondria divide by **fission**.

**Function:** mitochondria are the sites of **aerobic respiration**. They produce cellular energy as **ATP**, hence are called the 'power houses' of the cell.

**Chloroplasts: characteristics**

1. Found mostly in the mesophyll cells of leaves; lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or ribbon-like, 5-10 µm long and 2-4 µm wide; from 1 per cell (Chlamydomonas) to 20-40 per cell in the mesophyll.
2. Bounded by two membranes; the **inner membrane** is relatively less permeable.
3. The space enclosed by the inner membrane is the **stroma**. It contains flattened membranous sacs, the **thylakoids**, stacked like piles of coins into **grana**, and joined across grana by **stroma lamellae**. Each thylakoid encloses a lumen.
4. **Chlorophyll** pigments are present in the thylakoids.
5. The stroma contains enzymes for the synthesis of carbohydrates and proteins, small double-stranded circular **DNA** and **70S ribosomes**.

**Function:** chloroplasts trap **light energy** for **photosynthesis**. The grana are the site of the light reactions and the stroma of the dark reactions.

**Labelled diagrams** (Fig. 8.7 and Fig. 8.8):

- **Mitochondrion (longitudinal section):** an oval, sausage-shaped body with an outer membrane enclosing a folded inner membrane. Labels: **outer membrane, inner membrane, inter-membrane space, matrix, crista**.
- **Chloroplast (sectional view):** an oval body with two membranes enclosing the stroma, in which stacks of discs (grana) are joined by thin tubules. Labels: **outer membrane, inner membrane, granum, thylakoid, stroma lamella, stroma**.
groundedIn: §8.5.4; §8.5.5; Fig. 8.7; Fig. 8.8 — mitochondria shape, size, double membrane, cristae, matrix with circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, fission, aerobic respiration and ATP; chloroplasts in mesophyll, size and number, double membrane, stroma, thylakoids, grana, stroma lamellae, chlorophyll in thylakoids, DNA and 70S ribosomes, trap light energy for photosynthesis; grana light reactions and stroma dark reactions from the chapter SUMMARY

stem: What are the characteristics of prokaryotic cells?
solution:
Prokaryotic cells are represented by **bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO**. Their characteristics are:

1. Generally **smaller** and **multiply more rapidly** than eukaryotic cells; they vary greatly in shape and size (bacteria: bacillus, coccus, vibrio, spirillum).
2. A **cell wall** surrounds the cell membrane in all prokaryotes except **mycoplasma**. Bacterial cells have a three layered **cell envelope**: glycocalyx, cell wall and plasma membrane.
3. There is **no well-defined nucleus**; the genetic material is naked, not enveloped by a nuclear membrane. The genomic DNA is a single circular chromosome, and many bacteria also carry small circular **plasmids**, which confer characters such as antibiotic resistance.
4. **No membrane bound organelles**, except ribosomes. The ribosomes are **70S** (50S and 30S subunits) and are associated with the plasma membrane.
5. **Mesosomes**, infoldings of the cell membrane, are characteristic of prokaryotes. Cyanobacteria also have pigment-containing **chromatophores**.
6. Reserve material is stored as **inclusion bodies**, not bound by a membrane (phosphate, cyanophycean and glycogen granules).
7. Motile bacteria have **flagella** (filament, hook and basal body); **pili** and **fimbriae** are surface structures not used in motility.
groundedIn: §8.3; §8.4; §8.4.1; §8.4.2 — bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma, PPLO; smaller and multiply rapidly; cell wall except mycoplasma; cell envelope; naked genetic material and plasmids; no organelles except ribosomes; 70S ribosomes; mesosome; chromatophores; inclusion bodies; flagella, pili and fimbriae

stem: Multicellular organisms have division of labour. Explain.
solution:
**Division of labour** means that in a multicellular organism different cells, or groups of cells, become **specialised to perform different functions**, instead of each cell doing everything.

1. A unicellular organism performs all the essential functions of life within its single cell.
2. A multicellular organism is made of many cells that differ greatly in **size, shape and activities**, and the shape of a cell varies with the function it performs.
3. For example, red blood cells (round and biconcave) carry oxygen, nerve cells (some of the longest cells) conduct nerve impulses, white blood cells (amoeboid) defend the body, mesophyll cells (rich in chloroplasts) carry out photosynthesis, and tracheids (elongated) conduct water.
4. Different kinds of cells form **tissues**; tissues form **organs** and organs form **organ systems**, each carrying out a particular function such as digestion or excretion.
5. Because each kind of cell does one job, the functions of the body are carried out more efficiently, and the cells depend on one another.
groundedIn: §8.1; §8.2; §8.3; §8.5.5; Fig. 8.1 — unicellular organisms perform essential functions of life; different kinds of cells form tissues; cells differ in size, shape and activities, shape varies with function; shapes of RBC, WBC, nerve cell, mesophyll cells, tracheid; chloroplasts mostly in mesophyll cells; BEYOND CHAPTER: RBCs carry oxygen, nerve cells conduct nerve impulses, WBCs defend the body, tracheids conduct water, tissues form organs and organs form organ systems

stem: Cell is the basic unit of life. Discuss in brief.
solution:
The **cell** is the **fundamental structural and functional unit** of all living organisms.

1. The presence of the cell is what distinguishes a living organism from a non-living thing.
2. **Structural unit:** all organisms are composed of cells. Unicellular organisms are made of a single cell and multicellular organisms of many cells.
3. **Functional unit:** unicellular organisms are capable of independent existence and perform all the essential functions of life. Anything less than a complete cell does not ensure independent living.
4. The cytoplasm of the cell is the main arena of cellular activities, where the chemical reactions that keep the cell in the 'living state' occur, and the nucleus holds the genetic material, DNA.
5. **Cell theory** states that (i) all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells, and (ii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

Thus the cell is the basic unit of life.
groundedIn: §8.0; §8.1; §8.2; §8.3 — the basic unit of life, the cell, in all living organisms; unicellular and multicellular; cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit; anything less than a complete cell does not ensure independent living; cytoplasm the main arena of cellular activities; nucleus with DNA; cell theory as understood today

stem: What are nuclear pores? State their function.
solution:
**Nuclear pores** are minute pores at which the **nuclear envelope is interrupted**. They are formed by the **fusion of the two membranes** of the nuclear envelope.

**Function:** nuclear pores are the passages through which **RNA and protein molecules** move **in both directions** between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
groundedIn: §8.5.10; Fig. 8.11 — the nuclear envelope is interrupted by minute pores formed by the fusion of its two membranes; passages for movement of RNA and protein molecules in both directions between nucleus and cytoplasm

stem: Both lysosomes and vacuoles are endomembrane structures, yet they differ in terms of their functions. Comment.
solution:
Lysosomes and vacuoles are both part of the **endomembrane system** (with ER and golgi complex) because their functions are coordinated. Yet their functions differ: lysosomes are **digestive** vesicles, while vacuoles are **storage and transport** spaces.

| Basis | Lysosomes | Vacuoles |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Membrane bound vesicles formed by packaging in the golgi apparatus | Membrane-bound spaces in the cytoplasm, bound by a single membrane, the **tonoplast** |
| Contents | Rich in **hydrolytic enzymes** (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases), optimally active at acidic pH | Water, sap, excretory product and other materials not useful for the cell |
| Function | **Digestion**: their enzymes digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids | **Storage** of water, sap and wastes; the tonoplast transports ions and other materials into the vacuole against the concentration gradient; the contractile vacuole of Amoeba carries out **osmoregulation and excretion**; food vacuoles of protists hold engulfed food particles |
| Size | Vesicular structures | In plant cells may occupy up to 90 per cent of the cell volume |
groundedIn: §8.5.3; §8.5.3.3; §8.5.3.4 — endomembrane system includes ER, golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles; lysosomes formed by golgi packaging, rich in hydrolases active at acidic pH, digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids; vacuole bound by tonoplast, contains water, sap, excretory product, up to 90 per cent of volume, transport against gradient, contractile vacuole in Amoeba, food vacuoles in protists

context: Describe the structure of the following with the help of labelled diagrams.
solution:
The **nucleus** is a dense, membrane bound organelle that contains the chromosomes (the genetic material, DNA). Normally there is one nucleus per cell. The interphase nucleus has four parts:

1. **Nuclear envelope:** two parallel membranes with a space of 10 to 50 nm between them, the **perinuclear space**. It forms a barrier between the materials inside the nucleus and the cytoplasm. The outer membrane usually remains continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum and bears ribosomes.
2. **Nuclear pores:** at a number of places the envelope is interrupted by minute pores, formed by fusion of its two membranes, through which RNA and protein molecules move in both directions.
3. **Nucleoplasm (nuclear matrix):** contains the nucleolus and chromatin.
4. **Nucleolus:** one or more spherical bodies, **not membrane bound**, so their content is continuous with the nucleoplasm. It is the site of active **ribosomal RNA synthesis**; larger and more numerous nucleoli occur in cells actively making proteins.
5. **Chromatin:** a loose network of nucleoprotein fibres made of DNA, basic proteins called **histones**, some non-histone proteins and RNA. During cell division it forms structured **chromosomes**.

**Labelled diagram** (Fig. 8.11): a round nucleus bounded by a double nuclear membrane interrupted by pores, with a dark nucleolus inside the granular nucleoplasm. Labels: **nucleoplasm, nucleolus, nuclear pore, nuclear membrane** (with chromatin and perinuclear space).
groundedIn: §8.3; §8.5.10; Fig. 8.11 — nucleus is a dense membrane bound structure containing chromosomes with DNA; double nuclear envelope with perinuclear space of 10 to 50 nm, outer membrane continuous with ER bearing ribosomes; nuclear pores; nucleoplasm with nucleolus and chromatin; nucleolus not membrane bound, site of rRNA synthesis; chromatin of DNA, histones, non-histone proteins and RNA

context: Describe the structure of the following with the help of labelled diagrams.
solution:
The **centrosome** is a non-membrane bound organelle, found in animal cells, that usually contains **two cylindrical centrioles**.

1. The two centrioles are surrounded by amorphous **pericentriolar materials**.
2. The two centrioles lie **perpendicular** to each other.
3. Each centriole has a **cartwheel** organisation. It is made up of **nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils** of **tubulin** protein, and each peripheral fibril is a **triplet**. The adjacent triplets are linked.
4. The central part of the proximal region of the centriole is proteinaceous and is called the **hub**. The hub is connected to the tubules of the peripheral triplets by **radial spokes** made of protein.
5. The centrioles form the **basal body** of cilia or flagella, and the **spindle fibres** that give rise to the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells.

**Labelled diagram:** two short cylinders placed at right angles to each other, embedded in pericentriolar material; a cross-section of one centriole shows a cartwheel with nine peripheral triplets of microtubules around a central hub joined to them by radial spokes. Labels: **centriole, pericentriolar material, peripheral triplet fibril, hub, radial spoke**.
groundedIn: §8.3; §8.5.9 — centrosome a non-membrane bound organelle of animal cells; two cylindrical centrioles perpendicular to each other, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar materials; cartwheel organisation, nine peripheral triplet fibrils of tubulin, hub, radial spokes; basal body of cilia and flagella, spindle fibres

stem: What is a centromere? How does the position of centromere form the basis of classification of chromosomes. Support your answer with a diagram showing the position of centromere on different types of chromosomes.
solution:
The **centromere** is the **primary constriction** of a chromosome. It holds the **two chromatids** of the chromosome together, and disc shaped structures called **kinetochores** are present on its sides.

The position of the centromere decides the lengths of the two arms of a chromosome, so chromosomes are classified into **four types** on this basis:

| Type | Position of centromere | Arms |
|---|---|---|
| **Metacentric** | Middle of the chromosome | Two equal arms |
| **Sub-metacentric** | Slightly away from the middle | One shorter arm and one longer arm |
| **Acrocentric** | Close to one end | One extremely short arm and one very long arm |
| **Telocentric** | Terminal (at the very end) | Arms lie almost entirely on one side of the centromere |

**Diagram** (Fig. 8.13): four chromosomes drawn side by side, each with two chromatids joined at a dot-like centromere. From left to right the centromere moves from the middle (metacentric) to slightly off-centre (sub-metacentric), close to one end (acrocentric) and to the very end (telocentric). Labels: **centromere, short arm, long arm**, and on the metacentric chromosome a **satellite** with its **secondary constriction**.
groundedIn: §8.5.10; Fig. 8.12; Fig. 8.13 — centromere is the primary constriction, holds two chromatids, kinetochores on its sides; metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric and telocentric by centromere position; secondary constriction and satellite
